decks.title: Sound and Wave Motion — Part 1: Waves and the speed of sound
goals: Compare transverse and longitudinal waves and explain why sound in air is longitudinal
Describe the experiment that shows sound needs a medium
Compare the speed of sound in solids, liquids and gases and state the factors that affect it

slides.heading: Waves and sound
slides.body_md: Part 1: a wave carries energy, not matter. We meet the two kinds of mechanical wave, then ask what sound needs in order to travel and how fast it goes.

visual.alt: Flow: wave motion, transverse and longitudinal waves, sound needs a medium, speed of sound

slides.narration: A wave is a way of sending energy from one place to another. This part looks at the two kinds of mechanical wave, at what sound needs to travel, and at how its speed changes from one material to another.

slides.heading: What is a wave?
slides.body_md: A **wave** is a disturbance that travels through a medium and carries **energy**. The particles only **vibrate about their positions**; the medium does not move along with the wave. Waves that need a medium are **mechanical waves**.

visual.alt: Table showing which waves need a medium

slides.narration: When a stadium crowd does a wave, each person only stands up and sits down, yet the wave runs around the whole stadium. Energy travels, people stay. Sound, rope waves and ripples need a medium. Light does not.

slides.heading: Transverse waves
slides.body_md: In a **transverse wave** the particles vibrate **at right angles** to the direction in which the wave moves. The wave is a train of **crests** and **troughs**. The **wavelength** is the distance between two consecutive crests; the **amplitude** is the greatest displacement from the rest line.

visual.alt: A transverse wave with a crest, a trough, the amplitude and the wavelength marked

slides.narration: Shake one end of a rope up and down. The wave runs along the rope, but each bit of rope moves up and down, at right angles to the wave. The raised parts are crests, the dipped parts are troughs.

slides.heading: Longitudinal waves
slides.body_md: In a **longitudinal wave** the particles vibrate **along** the direction of travel. The wave is a train of **compressions** (crowded, high pressure) and **rarefactions** (spread out, low pressure). Sound in air is longitudinal.

slides.heading: Speed of sound in solids, liquids and gases
slides.body_md: Sound is fastest in **solids**, slower in **liquids** and slowest in **gases**. The values used here are 340 m s⁻¹ in air, 1500 m s⁻¹ in water and 5100 m s⁻¹ in iron. (Books give slightly different values; the question states the one to use.)

slides.heading: What changes the speed of sound in air?
slides.body_md: In air the speed **rises with temperature** and is **greater in humid air** than in dry air. It does **not** depend on loudness, pitch or frequency, and at constant temperature not on the pressure.

rows: increases (about 0.6 m s⁻¹ per degree Celsius)

visual.alt: Table of the factors affecting the speed of sound in air

slides.narration: Warm air carries sound faster than cold air. Moist air carries it faster than dry air, because water vapour makes the air lighter. Loudness and pitch have no effect on the speed at all.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: two sounds from one tap
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A worker taps one end of an iron rail of length 1020 m. A friend at the other end hears two sounds. Find the gap between them. (Air 340 m s⁻¹, iron 5100 m s⁻¹.)

**Step 1.** Time through the rail $= \dfrac{1020}{5100} = 0.2$ s.

**Step 2.** Time through the air $= \dfrac{1020}{340} = 3$ s.

**Step 3.** Gap $= 3 - 0.2 = 2.8$ s.

visual.alt: Table of the times taken by the sound in iron and in air

slides.narration: Find the time for each path separately, using time equals distance divided by speed. The sound through the iron arrives first. The gap between the two sounds is the difference of the two times.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the same time in two media
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A sound lasts 5 s on its way. How far does it travel in that time in (a) air and (b) water? (Air 340 m s⁻¹, water 1500 m s⁻¹.)

**Step 1.** Air: $d = vt = 340 \times 5 = 1700$ m.

**Step 2.** Water: $d = 1500 \times 5 = 7500$ m.

**Step 3.** In the same time the sound goes much further in water, because it is faster there.

visual.alt: Table of the distances covered by sound in five seconds in air and in water

slides.narration: Distance is speed multiplied by time. For the same time, the medium with the greater speed gives the greater distance. Water carries the sound more than four times as far as air in these five seconds.

slides.heading: Frequency, wavelength and speed
slides.body_md: Part 2: how fast a wave moves follows from how often it vibrates and how long each wave is. Then we compare sound with light and classify sounds by frequency.

visual.alt: Flow: frequency and wavelength, wave equation, thunder, ultrasound

slides.narration: This part joins frequency, wavelength and speed in one short equation, uses sound and light to measure the distance of a storm, and then sorts sounds into infrasonic, audible and ultrasonic.

slides.heading: Amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period
slides.body_md: **Wavelength** λ: distance between consecutive crests. **Frequency** f: vibrations per second (hertz). **Time period** T: time for one vibration, **T = 1 ÷ f**. The **amplitude** is the greatest displacement from the rest line.

visual.alt: A transverse wave with points A to F lettered

slides.narration: In this wave the distance from the first crest to the next is one wavelength. Frequency counts the vibrations each second. The time period is the time for one vibration, and it is the reciprocal of the frequency.

slides.heading: The wave equation
slides.body_md:
In one time period $T$ the wave advances one wavelength $\lambda$, so speed $= \dfrac{\lambda}{T}$. Since $T = \dfrac{1}{f}$:

$$v = f \lambda$$

The **frequency is fixed by the source**; the speed depends on the medium; so the wavelength changes when the medium changes.

visual.alt: Table of the quantities in the wave equation with their symbols and units

slides.narration: The speed of a wave is the frequency multiplied by the wavelength. The source fixes the frequency. The medium fixes the speed. So when a wave enters a new medium, the wavelength is the quantity that changes.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a wave on a slinky
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The first and the sixth compression of a slinky wave are 1.5 m apart. The source vibrates 8 times a second. Find the wave speed.

**Step 1.** Five wavelengths in 1.5 m: $\lambda = \dfrac{1.5}{5} = 0.3$ m.

**Step 2.** $v = f\lambda = 8 \times 0.3 = 2.4$ m s⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of the slinky wave data and answer

slides.narration: From the first compression to the sixth there are five wavelengths, not six. Divide the gap by five to get the wavelength, then multiply by the frequency to get the speed.

slides.heading: Quick check: finding the speed
slides.body_md: Multiply the frequency by the wavelength.

visual.alt: Table giving a frequency and a wavelength

slides.narration: A wave has a frequency of twelve hertz and a wavelength of half a metre. What is its speed?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: one note, two media
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A 500 Hz note passes from air (340 m s⁻¹) into water (1500 m s⁻¹). Find the wavelength in each.

**Step 1.** Air: $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{340}{500} = 0.68$ m.

**Step 2.** Water: $\lambda = \dfrac{1500}{500} = 3$ m.

**Step 3.** The frequency stays 500 Hz; only the wavelength changes.

visual.alt: Table of speed, frequency and wavelength of the note in air and in water

slides.narration: Divide the speed by the frequency in each medium. The wavelength is much longer in water because the speed is greater, while the frequency, set by the source, is unchanged.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: how far was the lightning?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The thunder is heard 4.5 s after the flash is seen. How far is the lightning? (Speed of sound 340 m s⁻¹.)

**Step 1.** Light takes a negligible time, so the gap is the travel time of sound.

**Step 2.** $d = v \times t = 340 \times 4.5 = 1530$ m.

slides.heading: Uses of ultrasound
slides.body_md: Ultrasound is used for **ultrasonography** (images of the unborn baby and organs), **cleaning** delicate parts, **finding flaws** in metal castings and **measuring depth** under water. Bats and dolphins use it naturally.

slides.narration: Because ultrasound is gentle and travels in narrow beams, doctors use it to see inside the body. Factories use it to clean small parts and to find hidden cracks in metal.

slides.heading: Ultrasonic is not supersonic
slides.body_md: **Ultrasonic** and **infrasonic** describe the **frequency** of a sound. **Supersonic** and **subsonic** describe the **speed** of a moving body compared with the speed of sound.

slides.narration: Ultrasonic and infrasonic are about how high or low the pitch is, measured by frequency. Supersonic and subsonic are about how fast something moves compared with sound. A jet can be supersonic without making an ultrasonic note.

notes.title: Sound and Wave Motion — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Wave motion: transverse and longitudinal waves
sections.body_md:
A **wave** is a disturbance that moves through a medium and carries **energy** from one place to another. The particles of the medium only vibrate about their mean positions; the **medium itself does not travel** with the wave. Waves that need a material medium are **mechanical waves** (waves on a string, water ripples, sound).

- In a **transverse wave** the particles vibrate **at right angles** to the direction in which the wave travels. The wave is made of **crests** and **troughs**. Example: a wave on a stretched rope or a slinky shaken sideways.
- In a **longitudinal wave** the particles vibrate **along** the direction in which the wave travels. The wave is made of **compressions** (particles crowded together, high pressure) and **rarefactions** (particles spread apart, low pressure). Example: a slinky pushed and pulled along its length.

**Sound in air is a longitudinal wave.** A vibrating source such as a tuning fork pushes the air layers next to it to form a compression, then pulls back to leave a rarefaction. The pattern moves outward while each air particle only moves to and fro along the direction of travel.

Light is not a mechanical wave; it needs no medium.

key_terms.definition_md: A disturbance that travels through a medium and carries energy without carrying the medium with it.
A wave in which the particles of the medium vibrate perpendicular to the direction of travel of the wave.
A wave in which the particles of the medium vibrate parallel to the direction of travel of the wave.

sections.heading: 2. Sound needs a medium; speed of sound
sections.body_md:
Sound is produced by a **vibrating body** and needs a **material medium** to travel. In the **bell-jar experiment** an electric bell rings inside a sealed jar. As the air is pumped out, the sound grows fainter and fainter, although the hammer can still be seen striking; in a good vacuum it can hardly be heard. When air is let back, the sound returns. So sound **cannot travel through a vacuum** (this is why astronauts on the Moon talk by radio).

Sound travels in solids, liquids and gases. Its speed is **greatest in solids, less in liquids and least in gases**, because the particles of a solid respond to a push most quickly. Typical values used in this chapter: air about 340 m s⁻¹ (room temperature), water about 1500 m s⁻¹, iron about 5100 m s⁻¹. Books quote slightly different values (air 330 to 344 m s⁻¹); a question always states the value to use.

**Factors that change the speed of sound in air**
- **Temperature:** the speed **increases** as the air gets hotter (about 0.6 m s⁻¹ for every degree Celsius, an approximate rule).
- **Humidity:** the speed is **greater in moist air** than in dry air at the same temperature, because water vapour makes air less dense.
- **Nature of the medium:** different media, different speeds.

The speed does **not** depend on the loudness, the frequency or the pitch of the sound, and (at constant temperature) not on the air pressure. Wind carrying the air along changes the time taken to reach a listener, not the speed of sound relative to the air.

key_terms.definition_md: The material through which a wave travels.
Space with no matter in it; sound cannot pass through it.

sections.heading: 3. Frequency, wavelength, time period and speed
sections.body_md:
For a wave:
- **Amplitude** is the maximum displacement of a particle from its rest position.
- **Wavelength** λ is the distance between two consecutive crests (or troughs, compressions or rarefactions). SI unit: metre.
- **Frequency** f is the number of complete vibrations (or waves passing a point) per second. SI unit: **hertz** (Hz).
- **Time period** T is the time for one complete vibration: **T = 1 ÷ f**, in seconds.

In one time period the wave moves forward by one wavelength, so **speed = wavelength ÷ time period**, that is

**v = f × λ**

The frequency is fixed by the **source**. When a sound passes from one medium to another its frequency stays the same, while its speed and wavelength change (for a 500 Hz sound the wavelength is 0.68 m in air and 3 m in water).

*Worked case:* a slinky wave has 5 wavelengths in 1.5 m, so λ = 0.3 m; with f = 8 Hz the speed is 8 × 0.3 = 2.4 m s⁻¹.

key_terms.definition_md: The distance between two consecutive crests, troughs, compressions or rarefactions of a wave.
The number of complete vibrations made by a source (or waves passing a point) in one second; unit hertz.
The time taken for one complete vibration; T = 1 / f.

sections.heading: 4. Sound and light: thunder and lightning
sections.body_md:
Light travels at about **3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹**, nearly nine hundred thousand times faster than sound in air (340 m s⁻¹). In a thunderstorm the flash and the thunder start at the same moment, but we **see** the flash almost at once and **hear** the thunder later.

Distance of the lightning = speed of sound × time gap between seeing the flash and hearing the thunder.

For a gap of 4.5 s the lightning is 340 × 4.5 = 1530 m away. The light took only about 5.1 millionths of a second to cover that distance, so its travel time is neglected. The same idea is used to find the distance of a distant firework or a gun fired far away.

key_terms.definition_md: The sound produced by lightning; it reaches us later than the flash because sound is much slower than light.

sections.heading: 5. Infrasonic, audible and ultrasonic sound
sections.body_md:
The human ear detects sounds of frequency from about **20 Hz to 20 000 Hz** (20 kHz): this is the **audible range**. The upper limit falls with age.

- **Infrasonic** sound has frequency **below 20 Hz**. Sources: earthquakes, elephants, whales. Humans cannot hear it, but some animals can and may sense a coming earthquake.
- **Ultrasonic** sound has frequency **above 20 000 Hz**. Sources: bats, dolphins, dog whistles, electronic devices.

**Uses of ultrasound:** ultrasonography (images of the unborn baby and organs), cleaning of delicate parts and jewellery, finding cracks and flaws in metal parts, and measuring depth under water. Bats use it to find insects in the dark. Ultrasound is preferred in medicine because it is non-ionising and gentle on tissue.

**Do not confuse the words.** *Ultrasonic* and *infrasonic* describe the **frequency** of a sound. *Supersonic* describes a **speed greater than the speed of sound** (a fighter jet), and *subsonic* describes a speed **less than** the speed of sound (a cyclist, a passenger plane). A supersonic aircraft does not have to make ultrasonic sound.

Describes a speed greater than the speed of sound in the medium.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying "sound is a transverse wave" or that the particles travel with the wave; they only vibrate about their positions.
- Mixing up the two terms: *ultrasonic* is about frequency and *supersonic* is about speed (the same for *infrasonic* and *subsonic*).
- Giving the speed of sound in air without a value or unit; always state the value taken (for example 340 m s⁻¹).
- Writing v = f λ with λ in centimetres and getting the speed in the wrong unit.
- Forgetting that the frequency does not change when sound goes from one medium into another.
- In a thunder question, using the speed of light for the delay or forgetting to multiply the time gap by the speed of sound.
- Saying "sound travels faster in dry air" or "faster at night"; warm, moist air carries sound faster.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a definition, a unit, a range or a one-line reason.
- 2 marks: a numerical with formula, substitution and unit, or two short points.
- 3 marks: a short description (the bell-jar experiment) or a two-step calculation.
- 10-mark structured question: a situation with parts: classify waves or sounds, read a wave diagram or graph, use v = f λ and T = 1/f, a thunder or two-medium calculation, and one reason or application.

cards.front_md: What does a wave transfer from place to place?
cards.back_md: Energy (the disturbance), not the particles of the medium.

cards.front_md: Define a transverse wave.
cards.back_md: Particles vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel of the wave; it has crests and troughs.

cards.front_md: Define a longitudinal wave.
cards.back_md: Particles vibrate along the direction of travel; it has compressions and rarefactions.

cards.front_md: Give an example of each kind of wave.
cards.back_md: Transverse: a wave on a rope. Longitudinal: sound in air, a pushed and pulled slinky.

cards.front_md: What is a compression?
cards.back_md: A region where the particles are crowded together and the pressure is high.

cards.front_md: What is a rarefaction?
cards.back_md: A region where the particles are spread apart and the pressure is low.

cards.front_md: Why is sound in air a longitudinal wave?
cards.back_md: Air particles vibrate to and fro along the direction in which the sound travels.

cards.front_md: Which is a mechanical wave: sound or light?
cards.back_md: Sound. Light needs no medium.

cards.front_md: What does the bell-jar experiment show?
cards.back_md: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum; it needs a medium.

cards.front_md: Order of the speed of sound in solids, liquids and gases?
cards.back_md: Solids > liquids > gases.

cards.front_md: Speed of sound in air used in this chapter?
cards.back_md: 340 m s⁻¹ (books use 330 to 344 m s⁻¹).

cards.front_md: How does temperature affect the speed of sound in air?
cards.back_md: It increases as the air gets hotter.

cards.front_md: How does humidity affect the speed of sound in air?
cards.back_md: Moist air carries sound faster than dry air.

cards.front_md: Does loudness change the speed of sound?
cards.back_md: No. Speed depends on the medium and its temperature, not on loudness or frequency.

cards.front_md: Why can astronauts on the Moon not talk directly?
cards.back_md: There is no air to carry sound, so they use radio.

cards.front_md: Define wavelength.
cards.back_md: The distance between two consecutive crests, troughs, compressions or rarefactions.

cards.front_md: Define frequency and give its unit.
cards.back_md: Number of vibrations per second; hertz (Hz).

cards.front_md: Time period in terms of frequency?
cards.back_md: T = 1 ÷ f, in seconds.

cards.front_md: The wave equation?
cards.back_md: v = f × λ.

cards.front_md: What stays the same when sound enters water from air?
cards.back_md: The frequency (it is set by the source).

cards.front_md: Define amplitude.
cards.back_md: The maximum displacement of a particle from its rest position.

cards.front_md: Speed of light compared with speed of sound?
cards.back_md: About 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, nearly nine hundred thousand times faster.

cards.front_md: Why is lightning seen before thunder is heard?
cards.back_md: Light is far faster than sound, though both start together.

cards.front_md: How is the distance of lightning found?
cards.back_md: Speed of sound × time gap between flash and thunder.

cards.front_md: Audible range of a human ear?
cards.back_md: About 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.

cards.front_md: Define infrasonic sound.
cards.back_md: Sound of frequency below 20 Hz, for example from earthquakes and elephants.

cards.front_md: Define ultrasonic sound.
cards.back_md: Sound of frequency above 20 000 Hz, for example from bats and dog whistles.

cards.front_md: Name two uses of ultrasound.
cards.back_md: Medical imaging (ultrasonography), cleaning delicate parts, flaw detection in metals.

cards.front_md: Ultrasonic or supersonic: which describes speed?
cards.back_md: Supersonic: a speed greater than the speed of sound.

cards.back_md: Infrasonic: frequency below 20 Hz. Subsonic: speed below that of sound.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Sound waves in air are longitudinal.

**Reason (R):** In a sound wave the air particles vibrate parallel to the direction in which the wave travels.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Parallel vibration is the very meaning of a longitudinal wave, so (R) explains (A), option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? When a wave travels along a rope, the particles of the rope travel along with the wave.
questions.solution_md: False. The particles only vibrate about their mean positions; the energy travels on.

questions.stem_md: In a longitudinal wave the regions where the particles are spread apart and the pressure is low are called ___.
questions.solution_md: Rarefactions.

questions.stem_md: In a transverse wave on a rope, what name is given to the distance between two consecutive crests?

answer.model_answer_md: The **wavelength** of the wave.

questions.solution_md: Wavelength.

questions.stem_md: Match each term in Column A with its meaning in Column B.

match_right.text_md: Region of high pressure in a longitudinal wave
Region of low pressure in a longitudinal wave
Highest point of a transverse wave
Number of vibrations made in one second
Time taken for one complete vibration

questions.solution_md: Compression and rarefaction describe pressure in sound; a crest is the highest point; frequency counts vibrations per second; the time period is the time for one.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave.

answer.model_answer_md: In a **transverse** wave the particles vibrate **at right angles** to the direction of travel and the wave has **crests and troughs**; in a **longitudinal** wave they vibrate **along** that direction and the wave has **compressions and rarefactions**.

questions.solution_md: Direction of vibration; crests and troughs against compressions and rarefactions.

marking_scheme.step: Direction of vibration of the particles
Crests and troughs against compressions and rarefactions

questions.stem_md: A tuning fork is struck and held in air. Explain, in terms of compressions and rarefactions, how the sound reaches a listener and why it is a longitudinal wave.

answer.model_answer_md: When a prong moves **forward** it pushes the air next to it together and makes a **compression**; when it moves **back** it leaves a **rarefaction**. These regions move away from the fork one after another. The air particles only vibrate **to and fro along the direction in which the sound travels**, so the wave is **longitudinal**.

questions.solution_md: Forward stroke compression, backward stroke rarefaction; vibration along the direction of travel.

marking_scheme.step: Particles vibrate along the direction of travel

questions.stem_md: Two astronauts standing side by side on the Moon cannot hear each other speak directly because

options.text_md: the Moon is much colder than the Earth
sound travels too fast on the Moon to be heard
the pitch of the voice rises on the Moon
there is no air on the Moon to carry the sound

questions.solution_md: Sound needs a material medium, and the Moon has no atmosphere, option (d).

questions.stem_md: In the bell-jar experiment the hammer is still seen striking the gong after most of the air is removed, yet hardly any sound is heard. The correct inference is that

options.text_md: the hammer has stopped touching the gong
light is able to travel through air better than a vacuum
the bell keeps vibrating but the sound has no medium to reach the ear
sound is made only when there is air inside the bell

questions.solution_md: Seeing the hammer move shows the source is still vibrating, so the missing sound points to the missing medium, option (c).

questions.stem_md: A sound wave is sent separately through a block of iron, a tank of water and a room full of air at room temperature. It travels fastest in

options.text_md: all three at the same speed

questions.solution_md: Solids carry sound fastest, then liquids, then gases, option (a).

questions.stem_md: A drummer at the far end of a field is heard after the same time on every morning of a week. On one afternoon the air is much warmer than usual. On that afternoon the sound reaches the listener

options.text_md: only if the drum is beaten harder

questions.solution_md: Sound travels faster in warmer air, so it takes less time, option (a).

questions.stem_md: At the same temperature, the speed of sound in humid air is

options.text_md: the same as in dry air

questions.solution_md: Water vapour makes the air less dense, so sound travels faster in it, option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following does not change the speed of sound in air?
questions.solution_md: Speed depends on the medium and its temperature and humidity, not on loudness, option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Sound travels faster in iron than in air.

**Reason (R):** Iron has a much smaller density than air.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Sound is faster in a solid, so (A) is true; iron is far denser than air, so (R) is false, option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The speed of sound in air increases when the sound is made louder.

**Reason (R):** The speed of sound in air increases when the temperature of the air increases.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Loudness does not change the speed, so (A) is false; temperature does, so (R) is true, option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Sound cannot travel through a vacuum.

**Reason (R):** Light can travel through a vacuum.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but the ability of light to cross a vacuum does not explain why sound cannot, option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The speed of sound in water is greater than its speed in air.
questions.solution_md: True. Sound travels faster in a liquid than in a gas.

questions.stem_md: A long iron wire is stretched between two posts 2550 m apart. A listener at one post hears the sound of a hammer blow at the other post through the wire. Taking the speed of sound in iron as 5100 m s⁻¹, find the time taken by the sound to travel along the wire, in s.

Using the same data (distance 2550 m, speed of sound in air 340 m s⁻¹), find how much longer the sound of the hammer blow would take to reach the listener through the air than through an iron wire that takes 0.5 s. Give your answer in s.
questions.solution_md: Time in air $= \dfrac{2550}{340} = 7.5$ s; difference $= 7.5 - 0.5 = 7$ s.

questions.stem_md: A diver under water hears the sound of a ship's engine that is 3000 m away. Taking the speed of sound in water as 1500 m s⁻¹, find the time taken by the sound to reach the diver, in s.
The speed of sound in air is 332 m s⁻¹ at 0 °C and increases by about 0.6 m s⁻¹ for every 1 °C rise in temperature. Find the speed of sound in air at 30 °C, in m s⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: Rise $= 0.6 \times 30 = 18$ m s⁻¹; speed $= 332 + 18 = 350$ m s⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: A rock falls on the surface of the Moon in front of an astronaut. Why does she see the rock land but hear nothing?

answer.model_answer_md: Light reaches her eyes without a medium, but the Moon has **no atmosphere**, and **sound needs a material medium**, so no sound reaches her.

questions.solution_md: No air; sound needs a medium.

marking_scheme.step: Sound needs a medium, light does not

questions.stem_md: Name two factors that change the speed of sound in air and state how each affects it.

answer.model_answer_md: **Temperature:** the speed **increases** when the air is warmer. **Humidity:** the speed is **greater** in moist air than in dry air.

questions.solution_md: Temperature up, speed up; humidity up, speed up.

questions.stem_md: Describe an experiment to show that sound cannot travel through a vacuum.

answer.model_answer_md: Hang an **electric bell** by a thread inside a **sealed bell jar** joined to a **vacuum pump**, and switch the bell on. As the **air is pumped out the sound becomes fainter and fainter** although the hammer is still seen moving. When air is let in again the sound returns. Hence sound **cannot travel through a vacuum**.

questions.solution_md: Bell in a jar; pump out the air; sound fades; conclusion.

marking_scheme.step: Bell inside a sealed jar joined to a pump
Sound fades as air is removed
Conclusion: no sound in a vacuum

questions.stem_md: Arrange iron, water and air in the order of increasing speed of sound, and give the reason for the order.

answer.model_answer_md: Air, water, iron. A **solid** has its particles close together and firmly bound, so a disturbance is handed on from one particle to the next **fastest**; in a **liquid** it is slower and in a **gas** the particles are far apart, so it is **slowest**.

questions.solution_md: Air < water < iron; closeness of particles.

marking_scheme.step: Slowest in a gas with a reason

questions.solution_md: Since $v = f\lambda$ and $v$ is fixed, $\lambda$ varies inversely as $f$, option (d).

questions.solution_md: The frequency is fixed by the source; the speed and so the wavelength change, option (a).

questions.solution_md: The time for one vibration is the reciprocal of the number of vibrations per second, option (c).

questions.stem_md: Waves of frequency 4 Hz and wavelength 0.75 m are sent along a long rope. Find the speed of the waves, in m s⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: $v = f\lambda = 4 \times 0.75 = 3$ m s⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: A factory siren produces sound of wavelength 0.85 m in air. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m s⁻¹, find the frequency of the siren, in Hz.
questions.solution_md: $f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{340}{0.85} = 400$ Hz.

questions.stem_md: A bee's wings beat 12000 times in 60 s. Find the time period of the vibration of its wings, in s.
Find the wavelength in air of the lowest audible sound, of frequency 20 Hz. Take the speed of sound in air as 340 m s⁻¹. Give your answer in m.
questions.solution_md: $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{340}{20} = 17$ m.

questions.stem_md: A flute note has a wavelength of 0.34 m in air, where the speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. Find the frequency of the note, in Hz.
questions.solution_md: $f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{340}{0.34} = 1000$ Hz.

questions.stem_md: A tuning fork has a frequency of 250 Hz. Find the time period of its vibration, in s.
The SI unit of frequency is the ___.
questions.solution_md: Hertz (Hz), one vibration per second.

questions.stem_md: A note of frequency 500 Hz travels from air into water. State what happens to its frequency and to its wavelength, giving a reason for each.

answer.model_answer_md: The **frequency stays the same**, because it is fixed by the source. The **wavelength increases**, because the speed is greater in water and **λ = v ÷ f**.

questions.solution_md: Frequency unchanged; wavelength larger because speed is larger.

questions.stem_md: Define the frequency and the time period of a vibrating source, and state the relation between them.

answer.model_answer_md: The **frequency** is the number of vibrations made in one second (unit hertz); the **time period** is the time taken for one vibration. They are related by **T = 1 ÷ f**.

questions.solution_md: Vibrations per second; time for one; T = 1/f.

questions.stem_md: A wave of wavelength λ and time period T travels in a medium. Show that its speed is v = fλ, where f is its frequency.

answer.model_answer_md: In **one time period T** the wave advances **one wavelength λ**. So speed v = distance ÷ time = **λ ÷ T**. Since **f = 1 ÷ T**, this gives **v = fλ**.

questions.solution_md: One wavelength in one period; v = λ/T; f = 1/T.

marking_scheme.step: One wavelength travelled in one period
Using f = 1 ÷ T to reach v = fλ

sound travels through a vacuum more easily than light
the flash is nearer to the observer than the thunder

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** First case: **longitudinal**; second case: **transverse**.

(d) The **first case**, because the air particles vibrate **along** the direction of travel of the sound, making compressions and rarefactions.

questions.solution_md: Longitudinal and transverse; compressions and rarefactions; crests and troughs at right angles; the first, as air vibrates along the wave.

**(a)** The sound becomes **fainter and fainter**, and is hardly heard when most of the air is gone.

During a storm a child counts 6 s between the flash of one lightning stroke and its thunder. Later she counts 10 s for a second stroke. Take the speed of sound in air as 340 m s⁻¹ and the speed of light as 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

(a) Why does she see the flash before she hears the thunder? [2]

(b) Find the distance of the first stroke. [2]

(c) Find the distance of the second stroke and say which stroke was farther away. [2]

(d) Find the time taken by the light of the first stroke to reach her, in microseconds. [3]

(e) Using your answer to (d), state why this time can be neglected. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The flash and the thunder start together, but **light travels far faster than sound**, so the light arrives almost at once and the sound arrives later.

**(b)** d = v × t = 340 × 6 = **2040 m**.

**(c)** d = 340 × 10 = **3400 m**; the **second** stroke was farther away.

**(d)** t = 2040 ÷ (3 × 10⁸) = 0.0000068 s = **6.8 µs**.

**(e)** It is about **a few millionths of a second**, tiny compared with several seconds for the sound.

questions.solution_md: Light is faster; 2040 m; 3400 m, the second; 6.8 µs; negligible.

questions.stem_md:
A worker taps one end of a long iron rail of length 1020 m. A friend with her ear to the other end hears two separate sounds. Take the speed of sound as 5100 m s⁻¹ in iron and 340 m s⁻¹ in air.

(a) Why does the friend hear two sounds, and which one arrives first? [2]

(b) Calculate the time taken by the sound to travel through the rail and through the air. [3]

(c) Find the gap between the two sounds. [1]

(d) The tap produces a note of frequency 500 Hz. Find its wavelength in air and in iron. [3]

(e) State the frequency of the note in iron. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The sound travels along **two paths**, through the iron and through the air, at **different speeds**; the sound through the **iron** (a solid, faster) arrives first.

**(b)** Iron: t = 1020 ÷ 5100 = **0.2 s**; air: t = 1020 ÷ 340 = **3 s**.

**(c)** 3 − 0.2 = **2.8 s**.

**(d)** In air: λ = v ÷ f = 340 ÷ 500 = **0.68 m**; in iron: λ = 5100 ÷ 500 = **10.2 m**.

**(e)** **500 Hz**, the same, because the frequency is fixed by the source.

questions.solution_md: Two paths with different speeds, iron first; 0.2 s and 3 s; 2.8 s; 0.68 m and 10.2 m; 500 Hz.

marking_scheme.step: Iron first, because sound is faster in a solid

questions.stem_md:
A science club records the frequency of four sound sources and wants to classify them. Take the speed of sound in air as 340 m s⁻¹.

| Source | Frequency |
|---|---|
| Whale call | 12 Hz |
| Guitar string | 330 Hz |
| Cleaning bath for jewellery | 40 000 Hz |
| Fire-alarm tone | 3000 Hz |

(a) State the audible range of a human ear and classify each of the four sources as infrasonic, audible or ultrasonic. [4]

(b) Name the source that cannot be heard because its frequency is too high, and give one more use of that kind of sound. [2]

(c) Find the wavelength in air of the sound of the guitar string. [2]

(d) A jet aircraft flies at a speed greater than that of sound. State, with a reason, whether it is correct to call the sound of the jet ultrasonic. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The audible range is **20 Hz to 20 000 Hz**. Whale call: **infrasonic**; guitar string: **audible**; cleaning bath: **ultrasonic**; fire alarm: **audible**.

**(b)** The **cleaning bath**; ultrasound is also used for **ultrasonography** (or flaw detection in metals).

**(c)** λ = v ÷ f = 340 ÷ 330 = **1.03 m** (about 1.03 m).

**(d)** **No.** Ultrasonic describes the **frequency** of a sound; the jet's high speed makes it **supersonic**, which is a statement about speed.

questions.solution_md: Range; infrasonic, audible, ultrasonic, audible; cleaning bath, imaging; 1.03 m; no, supersonic is about speed.

marking_scheme.step: Guitar string and fire alarm audible
Supersonic is about speed, ultrasonic about frequency

questions.stem_md: When a wave travels through a medium it transfers

options.text_md: particles of the medium from one place to another
both the particles and the energy of the medium
energy from one place to another

questions.solution_md: A wave moves energy; the particles only vibrate about their positions, option (d).

questions.stem_md: Sound is always produced by a body that is
questions.solution_md: Every source of sound, such as a tuning fork or a drum skin, is vibrating, option (d).

questions.stem_md: The amplitude of a wave on a rope is the

options.text_md: greatest displacement of a point of the rope from its rest position
number of crests passing a point in one second
time taken for one complete vibration

questions.solution_md: The other options describe the wavelength, the frequency and the time period, option (a).
